subject: Vocabulary
description: Literary devices: simile, metaphor, alliteration, hyperbole, personification, irony

questions.stem: Identify the literary device: 'Time is a thief.'

options.option_text: Simile (uses 'like' or 'as')
Metaphor (direct comparison)
Alliteration (repeating sounds)
Onomatopoeia (sound words)

questions.explanation: METAPHOR = DIRECT comparison (no 'like' or 'as'); says one thing IS another. 'Time IS a thief' implies time silently steals our moments. Compare with SIMILE (uses 'like' or 'as'): 'Time is LIKE a thief' = simile. Other examples of metaphor: 'Life is a journey'; 'Her eyes are stars'; 'Education is the key to success'. INSIGHT — metaphors are POWERFUL because the brain unconsciously equates the two; reshapes thinking. Famous: Shakespeare 'All the world's a stage' (metaphor for life). EXTENDED METAPHOR = a metaphor sustained over many lines (e.g., Robert Frost's 'The Road Not Taken' — life as a forked path).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'She sells seashells by the seashore.' This is an example of:

options.option_text: Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration)
Alliteration (repeating consonant sounds)
Personification (human traits to things)
Metaphor (direct comparison) here

questions.explanation: ALLITERATION = repetition of CONSONANT sounds at start of nearby words. 'Sells seashells seashore' — repeated 'S' sound. Common in TONGUE TWISTERS, poetry, advertising (Coca-Cola, Mickey Mouse, Krispy Kreme). RELATED: ASSONANCE = repeated VOWEL sounds ('hear the mellow wedding bells' — Poe); CONSONANCE = repeated consonants anywhere (not just start) ('pitter-patter'); ONOMATOPOEIA = words that imitate sounds (buzz, hiss, splash, meow). INSIGHT — alliteration creates RHYTHM + makes phrases memorable. Why brand names use it: easier to recall.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'I have told you a million times not to do that!' is an example of:

options.option_text: Irony (saying opposite of meaning)
Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration)
Simile (using 'like' or 'as')
Metaphor (direct comparison form)

questions.explanation: HYPERBOLE = deliberate EXAGGERATION for effect (not literally meant). 'A million times' = many times. Other examples: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse'; 'This bag weighs a tonne'; 'I died laughing'. NOT the same as a LIE — both speaker + listener KNOW it's exaggerated. Used in: poetry, casual speech, marketing, comedy. INSIGHT — opposite of hyperbole is UNDERSTATEMENT / LITOTES (deliberate downplay): 'It's not bad' (= it's good); 'a few problems' (when there are many). Both add EMPHASIS via deviation from literal truth. Hyperbole adds DRAMA; understatement adds IRONY or modesty.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'The wind whispered through the trees' uses which device?

options.option_text: Hyperbole (overstatement device)
Personification (human traits to non-human)
Onomatopoeia (sound-imitating words)
Alliteration (consonant repetition)

questions.explanation: PERSONIFICATION = giving HUMAN traits / actions to non-human things (objects, animals, ideas). Wind doesn't literally whisper — humans do; attributing whispering to wind = personification. Other examples: 'The flowers danced in the breeze'; 'Time waits for no one'; 'Lady Liberty' (statue personifies liberty as a woman). INSIGHT — personification makes abstract or non-human things RELATABLE + EMOTIONAL. Common in poetry, fables, mythology. ANTHROPOMORPHISM = related — physically attributing human form (Mickey Mouse standing, talking). PATHETIC FALLACY = subset where NATURE reflects human emotion ('the rain wept all day for the lost soul').
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'Water, water everywhere, nor any drop to drink' (Coleridge) shows:

options.option_text: Hyperbole (overstatement) only here also
Irony (situational) — surrounded by water yet thirsty
Alliteration (consonant sounds) here also
Onomatopoeia (sound imitation) here also

questions.explanation: IRONY — when there's a contrast between expected + actual / surface + meaning. SITUATIONAL irony = events contrary to expectation. Sailors in OCEAN are surrounded by water yet DYING of thirst (sea water = undrinkable). Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798). Three types: SITUATIONAL (gap between expectation + reality); VERBAL (saying opposite of what you mean — close to sarcasm); DRAMATIC (audience knows what character doesn't, e.g., Romeo thinks Juliet is dead — audience knows she's faking). INSIGHT — irony adds depth, often tragic or comic. Common Indian example: rain-shortage in Cherrapunji, once world's wettest place — situational irony.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'My love is like a red, red rose' (Robert Burns) is a:

options.option_text: Metaphor (direct comparison form)
Simile (uses 'like' for comparison)
Personification (human traits given)
Hyperbole (a deliberate exaggeration)

questions.explanation: SIMILE = comparison using 'LIKE' or 'AS'. 'My love is LIKE a red rose'. Compare to METAPHOR (no 'like/as'): 'My love is a rose' = metaphor. Both compare; simile is EXPLICIT comparison, metaphor is IMPLICIT. Famous similes: 'busy as a bee', 'cold as ice', 'sly as a fox', 'as light as a feather'. INSIGHT — similes are gentler / less assertive than metaphors. 'She is like a queen' (suggests resemblance) vs 'She is a queen' (more declarative). EXAM TIP: search for 'like' or 'as' = simile; absence + still comparison = metaphor.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: 'The bees buzzed as the kettle whistled' uses which device?

options.option_text: Personification (human qualities)
Onomatopoeia (sound-imitating words)
Hyperbole (overstatement device)
Metaphor (direct comparison form)

questions.explanation: ONOMATOPOEIA = words that IMITATE the sound they describe. 'BUZZ' (bees), 'WHISTLE' (kettle), and others — bang, crash, splash, hiss, meow, oink, tick-tock, gurgle, sizzle. INSIGHT — onomatopoeia bridges sound + meaning; makes writing VIVID + sensory. COMICS use these (POW! BAM! ZAP!). DIFFERENT LANGUAGES have different onomatopoeia for same sound — dog barks: English 'woof', Hindi 'bhau', Japanese 'wan-wan', French 'ouaf'; rooster: English 'cock-a-doodle-doo', Hindi 'kukdu-koo'. Reflects cultural ear-perception. Greek roots: 'onoma' = name; 'poiein' = to make → 'name-making'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A character whose contrasting traits are deliberately used to highlight the qualities of the protagonist is called a?

options.option_text: Antagonist — the story's primary opposing villain
Foil — a character that contrasts with the hero
Deuteragonist — the story's secondary main character
Narrator — the character who relates the story's events

questions.explanation: A foil is a character whose traits (courage, honesty, etc.) contrast sharply with those of the protagonist, thereby highlighting the latter's qualities. 'Antagonist' is wrong because an antagonist opposes the hero but need not contrast their personality traits — a foil's defining purpose is that contrast, not opposition.

questions.stem: A narrative that opens directly in the midst of ongoing action, skipping prior backstory and context, is said to begin?

options.option_text: In medias res — launching straight into the action
Flashback — revisiting an earlier scene in the plot
Foreshadowing — hinting early at later plot events
Exposition — setting up background before action starts

questions.explanation: 'In medias res' (Latin: 'into the middle of things') is the device of beginning a narrative at a critical mid-point. Homer's Iliad and Odyssey are classic examples. 'Exposition' is the opposite — it deliberately sets up context before action begins, so it is a common but wrong choice here.

questions.stem: 'Dark clouds gathered as the funeral procession moved silently through the town.' The technique where natural elements mirror a character's emotional state is termed?

options.option_text: Personification — giving human qualities to non-human things
Pathetic fallacy — nature reflecting human emotional states
Symbolism — using objects to stand for abstract concepts
Imagery — language that appeals to the reader's senses

questions.explanation: Pathetic fallacy (coined by John Ruskin) is the attribution of human emotions to the environment — stormy weather for grief, sunshine for joy. It differs from personification (which gives human actions/traits, not feelings to objects) and from symbolism (which is a broader representational device not tied to emotional mirroring).

questions.stem: In a stage play, the audience learns the hero is walking into a fatal trap, while the hero himself remains completely unaware. This situation exploits which literary technique?

options.option_text: Tragic flaw — a personal weakness causing the hero's fall
Suspense — tension built around an uncertain future outcome
Dramatic irony — the audience knows more than the character
Foreshadowing — dropping early clues about later events

questions.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience possesses knowledge that one or more characters lack, creating tension. Shakespeare uses it extensively in Othello and Romeo and Juliet. 'Suspense' is tempting but suspense is the reader's anxiety about an uncertain outcome — dramatic irony specifically requires an information gap between audience and character.

questions.stem: The emotional release — specifically the purging of pity and fear — that an audience experiences at the close of a tragedy was described by Aristotle in his Poetics as?

options.option_text: Denouement — the resolution that follows the story's climax
Hubris — the excessive pride that drives a character to ruin
Catharsis — emotional purging felt at the end of tragedy
Nemesis — divine punishment for a character's arrogance

questions.explanation: Aristotle in the Poetics (Chapter 6) defined catharsis as the purgation (katharsis) of pity and fear through tragic drama. 'Denouement' is wrong because it refers to the plot's untangling, not the emotional experience of the audience. 'Hubris' and 'nemesis' describe causes of tragedy, not its effect on the viewer.

questions.stem: When a poet deliberately lets a sentence or image run past the end of a line without any grammatical pause and continue on to the next line, the technique is called?

options.option_text: Caesura — a strong deliberate pause placed within a verse line
Enjambment — carrying a sentence across consecutive line breaks
End-stopped line — a line concluding at a full grammatical pause
Couplet — a pair of consecutive lines that share a rhyme

questions.explanation: Enjambment (from French enjamber, 'to straddle') keeps the syntactic unit incomplete at the line-end, propelling the reader forward. It is the direct opposite of an 'end-stopped line'. 'Caesura' is a pause within a line, not at its end, making it the most tempting wrong answer — both involve line-level rhythm but in opposite ways.

questions.stem: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets.' The repetition of 'we shall fight' at the START of each successive clause is a rhetorical device called?

options.option_text: Epistrophe — repeating a word or phrase at the clause's end
Chiasmus — reversing the grammatical order across two phrases
Anaphora — repeating a word or phrase at the start of clauses
Symploce — combining anaphora and epistrophe in one passage

questions.explanation: Anaphora (Greek: 'carrying back') is the repetition of a word/phrase at the beginning of successive clauses — Churchill's wartime speech is the textbook example. 'Epistrophe' is the mirror device (end-repetition). 'Symploce' combines both, making it the hardest distractor: the passage uses only start-repetition, so symploce would require end-repetition too, which is absent here.
